gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the inverter's own idle draw uses a large share of a weekend's battery. The Solar Lab measured 9.5 W on the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 and 13.6 W on the EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max with AC on and nothing plugged in. Over 48 hours that is about 456 Wh (22 % of 2,073.6 Wh) and about 653 Wh (32 % of 2,048 Wh). Load-tested usable capacity also differs by product: APH Networks got 2,028 Wh from the Elite 200 V2, StorageReview got 1,800 Wh from the DELTA 2 Max, and StorageReview got 920 Wh from the S2000 Pro.
standout_why: I read solutionenergy.com/off-grid/cabins, both cited Anker SOLIX blog guides and our current Dealectric page. None of the three rival pages has a measurement from a named reviewer or lab. They use maker ratings, NREL sun hours and flat derates of 85 % or 0.85. SolutionEnergy cites NREL ATB's 85 % round-trip figure, which is a reference value, not a product test. Our own page gives '1,910 measured', '950–1,030' and '920–1,380 in tests' without saying who measured them, and it assumes 10–20 W idle without a source. Neither ChatGPT answer cites any measured usable Wh or idle draw.
decides: It supports the Elite 200 V2 + 350 W kit as the pick and strengthens the case against the EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max as an equal. Elite 200 V2: 2,028 Wh measured (APH Networks) minus about 456 Wh of idle over 48 h (The Solar Lab's 9.5 W) leaves about 1,570 Wh for loads. DELTA 2 Max: 1,800 Wh measured (StorageReview) minus about 653 Wh (The Solar Lab's 13.6 W) leaves about 1,150 Wh. The two are rated almost the same (2,073.6 vs 2,048 Wh), but the BLUETTI keeps about 420 Wh more for the fridge. Without solar, neither covers a 2.3–4.0 kWh fridge weekend, so the panel is not optional. Switching the AC inverter off when nothing needs it, or running a 12 V fridge on DC, saves roughly 0.45–0.65 kWh per weekend. The AC180 measured 950–1,030 Wh (OutdoorGearLab, StorageReview), which keeps it at 'marginal with a fridge'. The S2000 Pro's 920 Wh at 350 W (StorageReview, 2023 test of the 1,500 Wh-rated version) and its shutdown at 55 % under a 2,250 W load (The Solar Lab) argue against making it a fridge-weekend pick.
